> there should always be a foreign-library based project

Yes: this, I think, will always be the case.

> and inside there a native subproject to source/build the native side

This might not _strictly_ be the case. It could be that you want to use a pre-made native library which is available for all platforms (kind of like zstd, but with binaries for everything - possibly openblas would be this way).
But yes, there is something that produces the native bits, either building or pulling them. This is currently the build plugin in some cases (still WIP), and some sort of script in others. But we will consolidate it to have all under the "build" plugin.

> You could certainly model that as a separate gradle plugin applied to the native subproject, but I would at least automatically apply that plugin to the subproject wherever we apply foreign-library, if the native directory exists.

There is another case, bringing the total to 3 I think:
- no native directory, no binaries to add to the distribution, (no need to verify compatibility). "Platform" (e.g.: Kernel32, libc, etc.)
- no native directory, but binaries to add to the distribution (need to verify compatibility). E.g. cuvs, openblas, ...
- native directory, binaries build from there and added to the distribution (verify compatibility "optional": we control compilation, they should be OK by construction, but good to have a safe guard if it is not "us" adding them). E.g. simdvec, simdjson. 

zstd is a mix of the second and third case. Like I said, we can (will) have 2 and 3 under the same plugin, but.. WIP.

All use foreign-library Java bindings, some need compilation, some need binaries copied to the distribution. This (binaries copied to the distribution) is where we need verification.
The current state is that we have a plugin for foreign-library, a plugin (almost, still one PR pending) for compilation. That we plan to extend to include the cases where we pull the binaries from somewhere (not compilation).

The last step (binaries copied to the distribution) is still done by native-libraries; we should get rid of it, that should be part of a plugin, not a central aggregator.

My 2c: we introduce the separate plugin from this PR. Then we extend it: this will become the "verify binaries **+ copy them to the correct location** plugin". It will work with binaries supplied in different ways (downloaded, built from source, etc.). Then we will have 3 plugins, and we apply them everywhere replacing custom scripts (shell and gradle). We observe how they interact with each other and if it makes sense we consolidate them. 

My gut feeling is that we could end up with 2 plugin classes, one for the Java side (foreign-library), one for the native side (compile/download, verify, copy). Could be just 1, but I have the feeling that it would be awkward. Don't know, we can try both ways. 

I would either proceed with this PR as-is, and then add the "native-libraries replacement" logic to it. Or, add the "native-libraries replacement" logic first. Thanks — this is a fair concern. I think there are two separate things to distinguish here: what the React regression test is proving, and what the end-to-end reproduction is proving.

The test in this PR is intentionally a narrow regression test for the React invariant: the completion `cacheSignal()` abort reason should not capture a stack. It goes through the Flight completion path and verifies that the actual reason stored on `signal.reason` has no stack frames. It is not intended to be the leak reproducer by itself.

The real-world reproduction is the one from vercel/next.js#84648. The workload does not retain the `cacheSignal` from application code; it uses a dynamic server component with a slow upstream and clients disconnecting while the render is in progress. Under sustained high concurrency, retained heap grows after forced GC. The same workload was independently reproduced on Next 16.3.1 / 16.2.12 with React 19.2.8 and Node 24.

The strongest evidence there is the A/B with `--stack-trace-limit=0`: without the flag, retained heap after the load rounds was 407–2264 MB; with it, 68–157 MB. The two sets did not overlap, and the `stackTraceLimit=0` arm showed no accumulating trend across rounds. This is what led me to the React `new Error()` / captured CallSites retention path rather than application-level retention.

I also agree that suppressing the stack globally does not isolate this exact React call site, since it affects other stack-producing paths as well. Looking into the history of this code block it seems that it was introduced to fix an issue where we would not auto scroll the text field to a visible position when first tapping on it https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/75604. At the time this change landed `_bringIntoViewBySelectionState` did not exist and was not called fom `formatAndSetValue`.

In it's current state `formatAndSetValue` does call `_bringIntoViewBySelectionState`. On iOS this handles both drags and long presses, while on Android only drags. 

The reason this bug is only presenting itself on Android and not iOS, is that when updating its selection, iOS always updates the moving edge to be the extent. Since `_scheduleShowCaretOnScreen` attempts to show the caret on screen (the extent of the selection), and we are always moving he extent, we always bring the moving edge into view as expected. On Android, if we move the start edge that is always going to move the `baseOffset` of the selection, similarly moving the end edge is always going to move the `extentOffset`. So when selecting backwards from the bottom of some long text, moving the start edge, `_scheduleShowCaretOnScreen` will always try to reveal the `extentOffset` even though we are moving the `baseOffset` and want to keep it in view.

A side note is that `TextFieldState._handleSelectionChanged` also calls `bringIntoView` when the selection changes because of a long press. Which would be called in `_handleSelectionChanged` before `_bringIntoViewBySelectionState` is called. These however do not conflict since on Android `_bringIntoViewBySelectionState` only handles drags and not long presses. On iOS we may be potentially calling `bringIntoView` twice. This should probably be addressed in a seperate PR.

The current regular expression `String\s+_generateSupportJs\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{(.*?)\n\}` is fragile. If `_generateSupportJs` contains any nested blocks (such as `if` statements or multi-line map literals) that end with a closing brace on a new line, the non-greedy `.*?` will match prematurely and truncate the function body, causing parsing to fail. A robust brace-counting approach should be used instead to correctly extract the entire function body. Additionally, the regex for matching string constants should support both single and double quotes to prevent future breakage if the Dart SDK code style changes.

```python
  start_match = re.search(
      r'String\s+_generateSupportJs\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{',
      compile_dart_content,
  )
  if not start_match:
    raise ValueError(
        'Could not locate `_generateSupportJs` in pkg/dart2wasm/lib/compile.dart'
    )
  start_idx = start_match.end()
  brace_count = 1
  end_idx = start_idx
  while brace_count > 0 and end_idx < len(compile_dart_content):
    char = compile_dart_content[end_idx]
    if char == '{':
      brace_count += 1
    elif char == '}':
      brace_count -= 1
    end_idx += 1
  if brace_count > 0:
    raise ValueError('Mismatched braces in `_generateSupportJs`')
  fn_body = compile_dart_content[start_idx:end_idx-1]

  feature_consts = dict(
      re.findall(

          fn_body,
      )
  )
```

This list ends on *"A drag n drop interface to upload files"* — the exact kind of controller that breaks when combined with the Turbo Streams section above, and the guide never covers that seam. A controller whose root element survives a Turbo Stream replacement never gets `connect()` called again, so per-element setup done there applies only to the elements present on page load. We shipped this twice: dead drop targets, and charts that stopped re-rendering after a morph. Silent no-ops both times, with green suites.

The example below deliberately uses bullet two from this same list, so it needs no third-party library.

````suggestion
* A _drag n drop_ interface to upload files.

### Controllers and Turbo

Turbo Streams and morphing replace elements in place. When a controller's root element
survives such a replacement, Stimulus does not call `connect()` again — so per-element setup
performed there applies only to the elements present the first time. Use the per-target
lifecycle callbacks instead; Stimulus calls them for every target as it enters or leaves the
DOM, including targets delivered by a Turbo Stream:

```js
export default class extends Controller {
  static targets = ["autogrow"]

  #observers = new Map()

  autogrowTargetConnected(textarea) {
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {
      textarea.style.height = `${textarea.scrollHeight}px`
    })

    observer.observe(textarea)
    this.#observers.set(textarea, observer)
  }

  autogrowTargetDisconnected(textarea) {
    this.#observers.get(textarea)?.disconnect()
    this.#observers.delete(textarea)
  }
}
```

Prefer `data-action` for ordinary event handling — morphing and Turbo Streams preserve it.
The lifecycle callbacks are for what `data-action` cannot express: creating an object for an
element, observing it, or wiring a listener that must be removed again.
````
